get.summary: See whether a session is a public agent and whether it can be made public now
get.description: Reads your own session, no PIN needed (making it public or private again is a `PUT` on the same address and needs the PIN). `blocked` says why it cannot be made public now; `crossTalk` is what the owner should be told before making it public (a public agent mixes conversations).

put.summary: Make a session a public agent, or make it private again
put.description: A kind of "letting someone in" (kind agent-exposure): needs the PIN, and the AI cannot do it. **A public agent mixes conversations**: when visitors ask it, they can read the main line's context, and answers may reveal the owner's own work; requests marked "act" go into the main line, and the question and answer stay in the main line. For an outward service where conversations stay apart, use a resident agent. Once it is public, who can call it is decided by the audience (by default open to everyone mutually recognised, with a card on the first call; `PUT /api/agents/:aid/audience`). Refusals (409): the session is archived (`session_archived`); it is an "ask-only" side branch or a resident agent's session (`not_publishable`); the session's identity skips all confirmations (`bypass_not_private`); this AI has no read-only mode and cannot accept "ask", while "act" is off (`act_required`: such an agent can be public only when act is allowed). Making it private again takes effect immediately: outside tasks in progress or queued are stopped (rejected), cards waiting for approval are voided, and its grants, audience and ask/act settings are cleared as well; side effects already produced are not rolled back. If it is already in that state, nothing changes.

post.summary: Run a native operation on a session (list models, fork, rewind, compact, etc.)
post.description: Asynchronous: answers the operation's id; query the result with `session.operationStatus`. The result of `fork` is in the new session (the answer's `sessionId`). Refused while the session has queued or running work. `args.count` for `rewind` is how many turns to rewind (1–10000, default 1). `fork`, `compact` and `rewind` (with `files: true`, it also needs "undo files when rewinding") require the session's AI to declare that capability (the snapshot's `features`); otherwise it answers 409 `capability_unsupported`, and `fix` says what to do.

post.summary: Change the configuration of the harness the session uses: config files, MCP servers, plugins, skills
post.description: Runs asynchronously like a native operation, with the result queried via `session.operationStatus`, but what it changes is the harness configuration under this profile (every future session is affected), so it counts as "manage" (`daisy:manage`), not a session operation.

post.summary: Open a terminal in the session's working directory
post.description: Runs asynchronously like a native operation; query its status with `session.operationStatus`, and read and write with `session terminal output` / `input`. Off by default on the outside face (the terminal switch).

post.description: Checks once against the update source the owner set (`updateSource` in runner.json; there is no default source); if there is a newer version, fetches it into the data directory's `update/incoming/` and reads its version number, without installing. post.summary: Switch to a new version (waits for idle; Daisy installed via npm)
post.description: Once fully idle: backs up the database first, keeps the current version's package as a fallback, runs `npm install -g` for the new version and checks that it loads, then restarts into the new version; if the new version is not running properly within 120 seconds, it rolls back automatically. Without `from`: the latest version in the source; `from`: a `.tgz` package on this machine. A version older than the one running needs `allowDowngrade`. Runs even when auto-update is off. Answers 409 `update_unavailable` when it cannot restart itself, is not a global npm install, or is already up to date.

post.summary: Set or change the PIN
post.description: The first set needs no old PIN; after a local reset it can only be set again on this machine's command line. Once a PIN is set, changing it needs the old PIN, and a wrong old PIN counts toward consecutive wrong tries just like getting a grant. After a change, all previously issued PIN grants stop working. Daisy stores only a verifier of the PIN. Until the PIN is set, Daisy starts no AI turns.

pin.description: The new PIN (6–128 characters; digits only is fine)

oldPin.description: The old PIN: required when one is already set

post.summary: Enter the PIN to get a short-lived PIN grant
post.description: A grant is valid for 5 minutes, and only for the credential that traded for it; a request that needs the PIN carries it in the `daisy-pin-grant` request header. 5 wrong PINs in a row lock entry (15 minutes; another wrong round 1 hour; then doubling each round, at most 24 hours); one right PIN clears it. The command line never caches a grant: every command that needs the PIN asks for it there and then, and the grant lives only in that command process's memory. The AI cannot call it.

grant.description: PIN grant: put it in the daisy-pin-grant request header

x-daisy-cli.exempt: The command line does not get grants separately: each command that needs the PIN prompts for it on the spot, gets a grant, and discards it after use (local-api.md §6), so the grant never lands in terminal output, shell history or files

post.summary: Reset the PIN locally (clears the PIN and all PIN grants)
post.description: Only done on the local command line (local credential); the web page, paired devices and the AI cannot call it. A reset clears the PIN and all PIN grants, withdraws trust in the external issuer and the stored owner tokens, turns off the outside face and voids its web sessions and one-time passcodes, revokes all outside grants, mutually recognised cards and paired devices, and records an audit entry; afterwards the PIN can only be set again on the local command line.

confirm.description: Confirm the reset: it withdraws trust in the external issuer and the stored owner tokens, and revokes all outside grants, mutually recognised cards and paired devices

get.summary: Read the event outlet incrementally by sequence number (long polling supported)
get.description:
Each event is a CloudEvents 1.0 event (docs/contracts/events.md): an AI asking for approval, an AI asking a question, someone's call waiting for approval — each with an "opened" and a "resolved" kind. Ordered by `seq`, ascending; `cursor` is the last event's `seq` on this page (equal to `after` when the page is empty), to pass as `after` next time; when `hasMore` is true, read on at once.

With no new event within `wait` seconds (at most 30) the answer is an empty page; a new event is answered at once.

Resuming after a disconnect: a subscriber saves `cursor` after it has handled a page and reads on from it after a restart; it may read the same batch again — deduplicate by `id`. An `after` older than the events still kept (already cleaned up), or larger than the highest sequence number this Daisy has written (its data was rebuilt), answers 410 with `code: cursor_reset`: take a snapshot first, then read on from the snapshot's `cursor`.

With nobody subscribed nothing happens: events are written all the same and cleaned up after 30 days; an "opened" event of a card not yet resolved is kept until it is resolved.

Each comes with its audience, whether act is allowed, and its number of cards waiting for approval and of always-allow grants. Read-only: the web page, paired devices and tokens an external issuer gave the owner need no PIN, the local command line does (a command-line credential may be the owner's AI); `daisy:grant` is still required, so the AI and visitors cannot read it.

post.summary: Issue a time-limited token to a third-party A2A client (daisy token)
post.description: A kind of "let someone in" (kind visitor-token): needs the PIN, and the AI cannot do it. The issued token: `iss` and `aud` are this Daisy; `sub` is that contact (yourself for `me`); `scope` is only `daisy:invoke`; `client_id` is `token:<jti>`; there is no `act`. Whoever holds it calls through A2A as that contact and still has to pass call grants (audience, allowlist, cards); one issued for `me` also only goes through the A2A entry and cannot reach the local API. The token appears only in this one answer; Daisy stores only the issue record (jti, for whom, note, expiry), not the token itself: whoever gets it can call as that identity, so keep it like a password. It is voided when the contact is removed or the PIN is reset.

post.summary: Make a pairing code (daisy pair): another device that enters it connects as the owner
post.description: A kind of "letting someone in" (kind device): needs the PIN; the AI cannot do it. A pairing code is valid for 10 minutes, works once, and only on the outside face (first turn on the outside face's listener or choose a relay, both with the PIN). The answer holds the code itself and a link (the code is after #, so it never reaches the request line or the logs; the web page draws it as a QR code). With the outside face's listener on, the link is direct (a relay operator could get a certificate for the relay's address), and the relay's link is given separately (`relayUrl`, `relayWarning`); with only a relay, the relay's link is given and `warning` says plainly that the relay operator can obtain the pairing code and the device credential; when the relay has only a self-signed certificate no link is given (`url: null`), just the code to type in on the device, with a warning not to click through certificate warnings. At most 5 unused codes at once; making another pushes out the oldest. 5 wrong codes from one source (the direct listener's address; through a relay, the address the relay reports) pause that source for 15 minutes (other sources go on); 20 wrong codes from all sources together void the codes of that period. `wasLocked` and `recentFailures` in the answer say someone typed a wrong code. Resetting or changing the PIN voids the unused codes and lifts the pauses too.

name.description: A name for this device; if empty, the name the device reports itself (the browser name) is used

post.summary: Another device exchanges a pairing code for a device credential and its first device session
post.description: Only on the outside face (the same for calls passed in through a connected relay). A right, unexpired, unused pairing code → the new device's record, a device credential (`ddev_…`, only ever in this one answer, kept on the device) and a device session (`dweb_…`, 12 hours). A wrong, expired or used code is always 401 code_invalid, without saying which; 5 wrong codes from one source pause that source (423 pair_locked); a code typed wrong 20 times in all while valid is voided. At most 10 calls per address per minute.

get.summary: Show the relay: which one is chosen, whether it is connected, the outside address, the certificate

put.summary: Choose a relay (or switch): Daisy connects out and stays connected, getting a fixed outside address
put.description: Requests arriving through the relay only reach the outside face, so choosing a relay lets anyone who can reach the relay knock on the outside face's door: it needs the PIN. The outside face's listener does not need to be on first (relay-only works too); the outside face's passcode is turned on automatically. Certificate: by default one is requested from Let's Encrypt (TLS-ALPN-01, passed through the relay); before it arrives, or if it cannot be obtained, a self-signed certificate is used, and then only Daisy-to-Daisy traffic works through the relay (they check the TLS binding statement), while third-party clients and browsers report an untrusted certificate.

url.description: The relay's own address, e.g. relay.example or https://relay.example:8443 (domain and port only)

acme.description: Request a certificate for the relay address from a certificate authority (ACME TLS-ALPN-01, Let's Encrypt by default). If off, only a self-signed certificate is used: then only Daisy-to-Daisy traffic works through the relay

acmeDirectory.description: ACME directory URL (https), Let's Encrypt by default; can be another certificate authority that supports TLS-ALPN-01

delete.summary: Stop using the relay: disconnect and remove the address from the card
delete.description: Connections going through the relay are cut immediately, and the card no longer carries the relay address. The key and certificate are kept (choosing the same relay again keeps the same address). It only narrows who can connect in, but still needs the PIN: a command-line credential may be the owner's AI using it through Bash, and it must not be able to quietly cut off the owner's reachability from other networks.

get.summary: TLS binding statement: "these TLS keys are mine", signed by this Daisy with its identity key
get.description: Public, no token needed (a2a-usage.md section 15.1). When another Daisy calls through a relay, it first fetches this, verifies the signature with the public key from its contacts, and compares it with the public key of the certificate on this connection; only if they match does it send its token: a relay can forge a trusted certificate for a subdomain, but it cannot sign this statement. Answers `application/jwt`: the header is exactly `{"alg":"EdDSA","typ":"daisy-tls-binding+jwt"}`, the payload `{ v: 1, id, spki: [...], iat, exp }`.
